newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bank of France seen cutting rates Thursday - poll.
newsitem.headline: Bank of France seen cutting rates Thursday - poll.

text.p: - The Bank of France is expected to cut its key intervention rate by five basis points to 3.10 percent after a monetary policy council meeting on Thursday, according to a Reuter poll conducted on Monday.

Nine out of 15 economists said they expected the French central bank to cut the intervention rate, which sets the floor for French money market rates, by five basis points and another predicted a cut of three basis points.

While the change in the composition of the Bank of France monetary policy council earlier this month boosted hopes for faster rate cuts, analysts said the Bank would be unlikely to make any dramatic move for fear of upsetting financial markets.

Council member Paul Marchelli, who has said France could cut rates without waiting for Bundesbank easing, said there would be no "revolution" after the appointments of Pierre Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard on January 3, both seen as potentially swelling the dovish ranks in the nine-member council.

Most economists expect the French central bank to close the gap between its key interest rate and the German repo rate, currently at 3.00 percent, at some stage this year and some expect French rates to move below German rates.
Hopes for French rate cuts sent interest rate futures to record highs on Monday.

The difference between French and German March futures contracts narrowed to eight basis points -- reflecting expectations of the gap between French and German rates at the end of March. The gap between June contracts fell to four.
Most of the analysts who said the Bank of France would remain on hold this week said more rate cuts were in the pipeline, possibly as soon as January 30, the next scheduled council meeting.
Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro in Paris, said while there was a chance of a cut this week he thought a move at the end of the month would be more likely.
"They want to appear more hawkish than they really are," Brossard said.
